lesson.menu_desc: An unlabeled hard drive, eleven files and one missing take -- modals of deduction: must be, might be, could be, can't be
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 17 -- That Must Be the Take
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Henrique Tadeu Alves da Silva | Lesson 17 -- That Must Be the Take
lesson.grammar_point: modals of deduction: must, might, could and can't

listenings.text: I work in the sound archive of a TV network, and half of my job is detective work. Last month, somebody brought me an old tape with no label. No date, no name, nothing. So I started with the clues. There is a hiss under the music, a soft, constant noise. That hiss is a telltale sign of analog tape, so this recording must be older than the year two thousand. Then I listened to the room. The voice is a little muffled, and there is no audience at all. So it can't be a live show. It must be a studio recording. The singer's voice rang a bell, but I wasn't sure. It might be a famous singer from the eighties, or it could be a backing singer who sounds like her. I had a hunch, but a hunch is not proof. Then, at the very end of the tape, somebody laughs and says, 'Okay, that's the one.' That voice was unmistakable. It was our old music director. So now I know it must be one of his sessions. And the date? I am still figuring that out.

Every mixing engineer knows this moment. You are listening to a mix, and suddenly you hear a strange noise, a low buzz, very quiet, only in the left speaker. Your first thought is always the worst one: the speaker must be broken. But wait. Don't panic. Do it step by step. First, I play a different song. The buzz is still there, so it can't be the mix. It must be something in the room. Then I turn off the computer screen. The buzz is still there, so it can't be the screen either. Now I have two ideas. It might be the cable, or it could be the air conditioning, which is on the left side of the room. One idea is a long shot, and the other is more likely. I turn off the air conditioning, and the buzz stops. That's the giveaway. So the problem was never in the music. My advice is simple: rule things out one by one, and don't trust your first guess.

extra_audio.text: I found the hard drive from the April session. None of the files has a label, so I listened to all of them. File seven can't be the final take, because the band stops in the middle. File nine might be the right one, but the vocal is a little muffled. File eleven has a count-in at the start and the full ending. So file eleven must be the take we chose.
